Anthropology

What is anthropology? The study of humans, past and present

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Anthropology is the study of human beings in all their variety: how our species evolved, how societies are organised, how languages work and how people lived in the past. It combines biology, archaeology, linguistics and the study of culture, and it is known for long-term fieldwork with the people it studies.

We run introductory anthropology sessions and an oral history lab for schools, colleges and adult groups, online or in person anywhere in India.

Anthropology meaning: where the word comes from

The word comes from two Greek roots: anthropos, meaning human being, and logos, meaning study or account. Anthropology is therefore the study of humans, but in practice it is defined less by its subject than by its approach. Many disciplines study people. Anthropology tries to look at the whole of human life together, across time and across the world, and to explain both what humans share and why they differ so much.

Three ideas sit at the centre of the subject. The first is holism: biology, environment, economy, kinship, belief and language are connected, so you cannot understand one without the others. The second is comparison: a practice that looks natural in one society is understood better when set beside how other societies handle the same problem. The third is fieldwork: anthropologists learn by living among people and taking part in daily life, often for a year or more.

What anthropologists study

The scope of anthropology is wide. An anthropologist might measure skeletal remains from an ancient cemetery, record the songs of a pastoral community, study how a village organises water sharing, map how a language changes between generations, or look at how a new highway changes life in a market town. What links these is the question of how humans live and how they came to live that way.

The discipline is usually divided into fields. You can read about them in detail in our guide to the branches of anthropology, but the short version is below.

  • Social or cultural anthropology: kinship, marriage, economy, politics, religion, law and everyday life in living societies.
  • Biological or physical anthropology: human evolution, primates, human genetics, growth, health and variation.
  • Archaeological anthropology: past societies studied through material remains, from stone tools to settlements.
  • Linguistic anthropology: language as a social practice, and how speech shapes and reflects social life.
  • Applied anthropology: putting anthropological methods to work in health, development, policy, museums and industry.

How anthropology works: methods and evidence

The signature method of social anthropology is participant observation, the core of ethnography. The researcher lives with a community, learns the language, takes part in work and festivals, and keeps detailed field notes. Interviews, genealogies, household surveys, life histories and mapping add to this. Good fieldwork depends on consent, honesty about the researcher's role and respect for the people who share their lives.

Biological anthropologists work with skeletons, fossils, body measurements and increasingly DNA. Archaeologists excavate and survey, then date and analyse what they find. Linguistic anthropologists record conversations and oral performance. Across all of these, the anthropologist tries to understand a practice from the inside first, in the terms people themselves use, before comparing it with other cases.

A short history of the discipline

Anthropology took shape as an academic subject in the late 19th century in Europe and North America. Early scholars such as Edward Tylor and Lewis Henry Morgan arranged societies on a ladder of supposed progress from savagery to civilisation. That scheme is now rejected, and much of 20th century anthropology was a reaction against it.

Franz Boas in the United States argued that each culture must be understood in its own history and context, and he built the four-field model still used in many universities. In Britain, Bronisław Malinowski's long fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands from 1915 to 1918 set the standard for ethnography, while A. R. Radcliffe-Brown developed the study of social structure. Later decades brought interpretive approaches, feminist anthropology, and sharp self-criticism about the subject's links with colonial rule.

Anthropology in India

India has one of the oldest traditions of anthropology outside Europe and America. Colonial administrators compiled caste and tribe surveys in the 19th century, often with crude racial assumptions. Indian scholars soon reshaped the field. Sarat Chandra Roy wrote detailed studies of the Munda and Oraon and founded the journal Man in India in 1921. The University of Calcutta opened the first anthropology department in the country in 1920, and the Anthropological Survey of India was set up in 1945.

After independence, M. N. Srinivas studied village life and coined the term Sanskritisation, Irawati Karve worked on kinship and physical anthropology at Deccan College, Pune, and many scholars studied tribal communities, caste, pilgrimage and urban life. Today Indian anthropologists work on everything from forest rights and migration to digital life and public health. The subject is closely linked to tribal communities of India, but it is not limited to them: anthropology studies cities and corporations as much as villages.

Why study anthropology today

Anthropology trains you to listen carefully, to notice assumptions, and to explain one group of people to another without caricature. Those skills are used in research, teaching, museums, heritage management, public health, development agencies, user research in technology companies, journalism and civil services. In India, anthropology is also a popular optional subject for the UPSC civil services examination, partly because its syllabus is well defined and links to many administrative questions.

It also gives a longer view of the present. The study of the Stone Age in India and human evolution reminds us that our species has lived in South Asia for tens of thousands of years, and that farming, villages and cities are recent developments in that long history.

How to start learning anthropology

Begin with a good introductory textbook and a few classic ethnographies, then read work on India by Indian scholars. Visit museums that show material culture with care, such as the Bhopal Tribal Museum, and practise simple fieldwork skills: observing a market, recording a conversation with permission, or collecting oral history in your own neighbourhood. Talaash Heritage runs an oral history and neighbourhood memory lab that teaches these first steps to students and adult groups.

Questions people ask

What is anthropology in simple words?

Anthropology is the study of human beings: how we evolved, how we live together, how we speak and how people lived in the past. It looks at humans as both biological and cultural beings and relies on close, long-term observation of real communities, along with fossils, artefacts and language data.

Who is the father of anthropology?

There is no single founder. Herodotus is sometimes called the father of anthropology for his descriptions of other peoples, Edward Tylor is often called the father of cultural anthropology, and Franz Boas is credited with shaping modern American anthropology. Malinowski is usually linked with the method of fieldwork.

What are the four main branches of anthropology?

The four classic fields are social or cultural anthropology, biological or physical anthropology, archaeology, and linguistic anthropology. Many departments also teach applied anthropology, which uses anthropological knowledge and methods to address practical problems in health, development, policy and heritage.

Is anthropology a science or an art subject?

It is both. Biological anthropology and archaeology use scientific methods such as genetics, dating and statistics, while social and linguistic anthropology are closer to the humanities and social sciences. In India the subject is offered in both BA and BSc programmes, depending on the university.

Where can I study anthropology in India?

Many central and state universities offer BA, BSc, MA and MSc courses in anthropology, including the University of Delhi, the University of Calcutta and the University of Hyderabad. Check each university's current admission notice, since course names, eligibility and entrance tests change from year to year.
